record.paper_title: Offline Reinforcement Learning: Tutorial, Review, and Perspectives on Open Problems
record.original_question: How should modern offline reinforcement learning be benchmarked so that evaluation datasets and simulations reflect the dataset statistics that make offline learning difficult, including concentration around particular trajectories, multimodal behavior policies, broad versus narrow behavior distributions, and compositional structure that allows transitive induction beyond any single trajectory in the dataset?

evidence.quote: While individual application domains, such as recommender systems and healthcare, discussed below, have developed particular domain-specific evaluations, the general state of benchmarking for modern offline reinforcement learning research is less well established.

However, even this formulation does not fully evaluate capabilities of offline reinforcement learning methods, and the statistics of the training data have a considerable effect on the difficult of offline RL (Fu et al., 2020), including how concentrated the data distribution is around a specific set of trajectories, and how multi-modal the data is.

When we also consider the capacity of neural networks to generalize, we could imagine this sort of “transitive induction” taking place on a portion of the state variables, effectively inferring potentially optimal behavior from highly suboptimal components. This capability can be evaluated with benchmarks that explicitly provide data containing this structure, and the D4RL benchmark suite provides a range of tasks that exercise this capability (Fu et al., 2020).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the offline reinforcement learning setting: an agent must learn a policy that maximizes expected discounted return in a Markov decision process M = (S, A, P, r, γ) using only a fixed dataset D = {(s_i, a_i, r_i, s'_i)} of transitions sampled from one or more (possibly unknown) behavior policies π_β, without any further interaction with the environment. The empirical performance of offline RL algorithms depends strongly on properties of D, including:

(i) concentration: how tightly the state-action visitation induced by D concentrates around a small set of trajectories;
(ii) multimodality: whether π_β is a mixture of qualitatively distinct behaviors;
(iii) coverage breadth: whether π_β has broad, near-uniform support over S × A or narrow, nearly deterministic support;
(iv) compositional / "stitching" structure: whether an optimal or near-optimal policy can be obtained only by transitively combining sub-trajectories from different trajectories in D, so that the learned policy outperforms every single trajectory present in D.

Design a principled benchmark suite (a finite collection of MDPs together with associated dataset-generating procedures and evaluation protocols) for offline reinforcement learning with the following properties:

1. For each axis (i)–(iv), the suite contains tasks with quantitatively controlled and measurable variation along that axis, and the chosen quantitative measures (e.g., a concentration coefficient, a modality count, an entropy- or coverage-based measure of breadth, and a formal measure of required stitching) are mathematically well-defined functions of (M, D).
2. The suite separates the difficulty contributions of (i)–(iv) in the sense that, for any pair of axes, there exist tasks in the suite that vary one axis while holding the other fixed up to a specified tolerance.
3. The evaluation metric (e.g., normalized return) admits a meaningful upper baseline corresponding to the best policy expressible from D under stitching, and a lower baseline corresponding to behavior cloning of π_β, and the gap between these baselines is non-trivial on the compositional tasks.
4. The suite is reproducible, in that the dataset-generating distributions are specified explicitly enough to be regenerated, and is large enough to support statistically meaningful comparisons of algorithms.

Provide such a benchmark, give the formal definitions of the axis-specific difficulty measures, and prove that the suite satisfies properties 1–4.
artifact.status_search_result: Benchmarking offline RL remains an active and unsettled research area. While the D4RL suite (Fu et al., 2020) and later additions (RL Unplugged, NeoRL, D5RL, ExoRL, V-D4RL) provide partial coverage of concentration, multimodality, coverage, and stitching, no benchmark to date provides quantitatively controlled, axis-separated variation along all of (i)–(iv) with the formal guarantees described, and recent surveys continue to list this as an open problem.

status_evidence.title: D4RL: Datasets for Deep Data-Driven Reinforcement Learning
status_evidence.snippet: Introduces datasets aimed at exercising properties such as narrow/biased data distributions and stitching of suboptimal trajectories, but does not formalize separated axis-controlled difficulty measures.
status_evidence.claim: Existing benchmarks address some axes but do not fully separate them.

status_evidence.title: NeoRL: A Near Real-World Benchmark for Offline Reinforcement Learning
status_evidence.snippet: Argues that prevailing offline RL benchmarks do not reflect realistic dataset statistics, motivating new benchmarks; indicates the question is unresolved.
status_evidence.claim: Benchmark design for offline RL remains an open problem.

status_evidence.title: A Survey on Offline Reinforcement Learning (recent)
status_evidence.snippet: Lists evaluation and benchmarking that captures dataset-difficulty properties as an outstanding challenge.
status_evidence.claim: Comprehensive axis-controlled benchmarking is still considered open.
